concepts.name: Deny by default and least privilege

questions.prompt: A new API route has no explicit permission policy. Which default is safest?

choices.text: Deny access until a policy grants it.
Allow all authenticated users until a complaint arrives.
Allow it when a browser hides the navigation link.
Trust the first request to establish its own permissions.

questions.explanation: Deny by default prevents gaps from granting access. Authentication, UI visibility and request-supplied claims are not a permission policy.

sources.title: Authorization Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Authorization should grant least privilege and deny access by default.

questions.prompt: A user changes `/orders/41` to `/orders/42` and receives another user’s order. Which control is missing?

choices.text: Encode both order IDs before showing them in links.
Move the order ID from the URL to a hidden form field.
Require a logged-in session but skip ownership checks.
Check permission for the requested order.

questions.explanation: Object access must be checked server-side. Encoding, hidden inputs and login alone do not establish ownership.

sources.title: Authorization Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Resource identifiers are not proof of permission; authorization must validate access to the requested object.

questions.prompt: A browser hides the Delete button from non-admins, but the API accepts their DELETE requests. What should change?

choices.text: Rename the route so it is harder to discover.
Trust the role value copied from localStorage.
Enforce the permission in the server endpoint.
Hide the button using a stronger CSS selector.

questions.explanation: Client-side restrictions are bypassable. The server must check the operation regardless of how a request is made.

sources.title: Authorization Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Permissions must be validated on every request and enforced server-side, including AJAX and alternate paths.

questions.prompt: A validly authenticated user lacks permission to edit a document. Which status describes that denial?

choices.text: 404 for every authorization failure because 403 is only for invalid credentials.
403 Forbidden.
401 Unauthorized because every denial means no login.
200 OK because the token signature was valid.

questions.explanation: 403 indicates that access is forbidden for an authenticated caller. 401 addresses missing or invalid authentication; valid identity does not make an unauthorized action successful, and authorization failures are not uniformly 404.

sources.title: REST Security Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: REST endpoints validate authentication and independently enforce access control; 401 and 403 represent different failures.

questions.prompt: A background worker only needs to read pending jobs. Which grant matches least privilege?

choices.text: Read permission for the required job data.
Administrator permission across all application resources.
Write access to every user record in the same database.
Permission to alter authorization policies during each job.

questions.explanation: The grant should match the worker’s task. Broad administrative and unrelated write access are unnecessary.

sources.title: Authorization Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Least privilege minimizes grants rather than relying on authentication alone.

questions.prompt: An application replaces sequential invoice IDs with UUIDs. What remains necessary?

choices.text: Remove ownership checks because UUIDs are unpredictable.
Trust any invoice ID that passes UUID syntax validation.
Grant access whenever a user knows the invoice URL.
Authorize access to each invoice.

questions.explanation: Opaque IDs reduce guessing but are not proof of permission. Syntax and URL knowledge are also not authorization.

sources.title: Authorization Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Authorization must validate object ownership rather than infer it from identifier complexity.

questions.prompt: Which access-control design practices follow least privilege? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Grant broad permissions first and narrow them only after a security incident.
Start with denied access and grant only required operations.
Review privileges as responsibilities change.
Give every service account administrator rights for convenience.
Treat authenticated status as permission for every action.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: Least privilege and deny-by-default policies should be established before incidents. B is correct: Explicit grants avoid accidental broad access. C is correct: Privilege creep can outlive the original need. D is incorrect: Broad permissions increase unnecessary access. E is incorrect: Authentication and authorization are distinct.

sources.title: Authorization Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Authorization should grant least privilege and deny access by default.

questions.prompt: Which object-access controls prevent identifier manipulation? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Check the caller’s permission for each requested resource.
Scope data queries to resources the caller may access.
Use a random identifier as the only authorization control.
Trust ownership values submitted by the browser without verification.
Test attempts to access another user’s object.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Authorization depends on the object and operation. B is correct: Authorized query scope reduces accidental exposure. C is incorrect: Hard-to-guess IDs do not replace permission checks. D is incorrect: Client input can be manipulated. E is correct: Negative tests expose missing object-level checks.

sources.title: Authorization Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Resource identifiers are not proof of permission; authorization must validate access to the requested object.

questions.prompt: Which requests require authorization checks? Select all that apply.

choices.text: An AJAX request for a protected resource.
Only the first request after a successful login.
Only requests using the main navigation route need permission checks.
Only requests whose buttons were visible in the UI.
A direct API call that bypasses the application navigation.

questions.explanation: A is correct: The transport does not remove authorization requirements. B is incorrect: Permissions must be checked on every request. C is incorrect: Alternate API paths must enforce authorization as well. D is incorrect: The server cannot rely on UI visibility. E is correct: Direct calls still access protected functionality.

sources.title: Authorization Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Permissions must be validated on every request and enforced server-side, including AJAX and alternate paths.

questions.prompt: Which distinctions matter for protected REST endpoints? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A valid signature grants access to every protected object.
Use 401 when authentication is missing or invalid.
Use 200 for denied actions so clients cannot detect failures.
Authentication establishes a trusted caller identity.
Authorization decides whether the caller may perform an operation.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: Token verification does not replace object authorization. B is correct: 401 indicates an authentication requirement or failure. C is incorrect: Successful status misrepresents the rejected operation. D is correct: Credentials identify the caller. E is correct: Permission depends on policy and resources.

sources.title: REST Security Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: REST endpoints validate authentication and independently enforce access control; 401 and 403 represent different failures.
